JavaScript Output Generated bindings are ES modules that import the runtime helpers from /wails/runtime.js : js Copy import { Call as $Call, Create as $Create } from "/wails/runtime.js" ; / ** * @param {string} msg * @returns { Promise < string > & { cancel () : void }} * / export function Send (msg) { return $Call. ByID ( 2042131923 , msg); } When generation runs with -names , $Call.ByName("pkg.Struct.Method", ...) is emitted instead — always fully-qualified , never just "Method" . Generated model classes use a $$source constructor pattern with per-field if (!("X" in $$source)) defaults, quoted field names, and a static createFrom(...) that runs JSON.parse on string inputs. Type Mapping Highlights Verified against internal/generator/render/ : Go TypeScript map[string]V { [_: string]: V } map[K]V (non-string K ) { [_ in K]?: V } (not Map<K, V> , not Record<K, V> ) []byte Uint8Array time.Time string (JSON ISO 8601) error (return position) rejected promise Reflection Note pkg/application/bindings.go is hand-written and uses reflect to drive method dispatch from a BoundMethod registry. Don’t read older claims of “zero reflection at runtime” too literally — the generator avoids reflection, but the runtime dispatcher uses it. 4. Runtime Invocation Protocol JavaScript Side ts Copy import { Call } from "/wails/runtime.js" ; await Call . ByID ( 0x7a1201d3 / * ChatService . Send * /, "Hello" ); // or, with -names: await Call . ByName ( "chatservice.ChatService.Send" , "Hello" ); The runtime helpers live in internal/runtime/desktop/@wailsio/runtime/src/calls.ts (call dispatch), events.ts (events), and friends — there is no invoke.ts or errors.ts in this tree. The exact wire envelope is encoded by calls.ts on the JS side and decoded by pkg/application/messageprocessor_call.go on the Go side; consult those two files together when debugging the bridge. Go Side pkg/application/messageprocessor_call.go receives the call message. Looks up the bound method by ID or name in pkg/application/bindings.go (driven by reflect ). Invokes the bound method and serialises {result, error} back to JS. Error Mapping Go JavaScript error == nil Promise resolves with result error != nil Promise rejects with an Error whose message is the Go error string 5. Calling JavaScript from Go The binding generator is one-way (Go methods exposed to JS). For Go → JS communication, use the event bus or run JS in a window: go Copy app. Event . Emit ( "chat:new-message" , msg) window. ExecJS ( `window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("ping"))` ) On the JS side, subscribe with Events.On(name, cb) from /wails/runtime.js . 6. Extending & Troubleshooting Unsupported Type Error text Copy error: field "Client" uses unsupported type: chan struct{} → wrap the channel behind a method API, or mark the field with //wails:internal so the generator skips it. Stale Bindings Generated output is overwritten on every wails3 generate bindings / wails3 dev / wails3 build . If IDE intellisense shows stale stubs, delete frontend/bindings/ and re-run the generator. The -clean flag (default true in current builds) wipes the bindings directory before each run. Performance Tips Avoid streaming large byte slices over the bridge — serve them via the asset server instead. Batch multiple quick calls into one method when latency matters. Prefer value receivers for small parameter structs to reduce allocations. 7. Key Files Map Concern File Generator orchestration internal/generator/generate.go Semantic checks internal/generator/analyse.go Collection (services, methods, models) internal/generator/collect/{service,method,model,struct,package}.go Render templates internal/generator/render/templates/*.tmpl Generated bindings location frontend/bindings/<full Go import path>/... Go side dispatcher pkg/application/bindings.go , messageprocessor_call.go JS runtime internal/runtime/desktop/@wailsio/runtime/src/{calls,events,index}.ts Keep this cheat-sheet handy when you trace a bridge bug. 8. Recap Collector scans your Go code → in-memory semantic model. Templates emit per-service ES modules and per-package model/index files. Message Processor dispatches calls on the Go side via the bindings registry. JS Runtime wraps it all in idiomatic promises with cancellation. All without you writing a single line of IPC boilerplate. That’s the Wails v3 binding system. Go forth and bind!

title: Build & Packaging Pipeline
description: What happens under the hood when you run `wails3 build`, how cross-platform binaries are produced, and how installers are generated for each OS.
text: wails3 build is intentionally thin : it’s a Taskfile wrapper that forwards extra build tags to the host project’s build task. The heavy lifting lives in the project’s own build/Taskfile.yml (generated by wails3 init ), in internal/commands/build-assets.go (which manages bake-time assets), and in internal/packager (Linux nfpm packaging) plus internal/commands/{appimage, msix,dmg/,dot_desktop}.go (per-platform installers). This page covers: The actual CLI entry-points The Taskfile-driven build flow Asset bake & build-info injection Packaging back-ends per platform Customising the pipeline Troubleshooting 1. Actual CLI Entry-Points text Copy wails3 build → internal/commands.Build (in task_wrapper.go) wails3 package → internal/commands.Package (in task_wrapper.go) wails3 generate build-assets → GenerateBuildAssets (in build-assets.go) wails3 update build-assets → UpdateBuildAssets (in build-assets.go) wails3 tool buildinfo → BuildInfoOptions (in tool_buildinfo.go) wails3 tool package → internal/packager (nfpm wrapper) wails3 generate .desktop → in dot_desktop.go internal/commands/task_wrapper.go : go Copy func Build (buildFlags * flags. Build , otherArgs []string) error { // forwards --tags / EXTRA_TAGS, then defers to a Taskfile target return wrapTask ( "build" , otherArgs) } flags.Build exposes a single flag — --tags (forwarded as EXTRA_TAGS= ). There are no -platform , -o , -skipbindings , -skip-package , -package , -ldflags , -verbose , -debug , -devbuild , -icon , or -clean flags on wails3 build . Cross-compilation, output paths, icons, etc. are configured in Taskfile.yml , build/config.yml , and the supporting wails3 generate icons / wails3 generate build-assets commands. build/build.json is not part of v3 — the config is Taskfile.yml plus build/config.yml . 2. Taskfile-Driven Build Flow A freshly initialised project ships a build/Taskfile.yml with namespaces roughly: Namespace Tasks (selection) darwin: build , build:universal , package , run , dev windows: build , package , run , dev linux: build , package , run , dev common: update:build-assets , generate:icons , generate:syso wails3 build invokes the host OS’s build namespace by default; the project’s Taskfile in turn shells out to go build with the host-specific flags. Building for another OS means running its task directly (e.g. wails3 task darwin:build:universal ), not passing a flag to wails3 build . The default output directory is bin/<APP_NAME> (no build/bin/ prefix). 3. Bake-Time Assets and Build Info Concern File Build-asset generation/update internal/commands/build-assets.go Build info printer (CLI: wails3 tool buildinfo ) internal/commands/tool_buildinfo.go — prints information; it is not an ldflags injector Production stub internal/assetserver/build_production.go — //go:build production Frontend bundles embedded via //go:embed in the application’s own package (e.g. next to main.go ) Windows resources ( .syso ) internal/commands/syso.go — generates rsrc_windows_<arch>.syso Windows MSIX internal/commands/msix.go + internal/commands/webview2/ macOS DMG inputs internal/commands/dmg/ Linux .desktop internal/commands/dot_desktop.go The CLI does not auto-bake bundled_assetserver.go for your application — internal/assetserver/bundled_assetserver.go is hand-written and wraps the embedded JS runtime under bundledassets/ . 4. Packaging Back-Ends Linux Linux packaging is driven by nfpm (not fpm ): internal/packager/packager.go wraps github.com/goreleaser/nfpm/v2 and exposes CreatePackageFromConfig(pkgType, configPath, output) / CreatePackageFromConfigWriter(...) . Generated projects ship myapp.DEB , myapp.RPM , and myapp.ARCHLINUX nfpm-style configs under internal/commands/ (used by wails3 tool package ). AppImage generation lives in internal/commands/appimage.go , which calls linuxdeploy + linuxdeploy-plugin-gtk (the plugin ships at internal/commands/linuxdeploy-plugin-gtk.sh ). There is no -package deb / rpm flag on wails3 build . Use wails3 tool package or the platform-specific Taskfile target. macOS darwin:package from the project Taskfile produces the .app bundle. DMG assets live under internal/commands/dmg/ ; a project can wrap the bundle into a DMG with hdiutil after darwin:package finishes (the Taskfile in newer templates includes a dmg helper). CFBundle identifiers, version, and copyright come from the -product* flags during wails3 init and from build/config.yml . Windows Windows packaging targets MSIX (not WiX/MSI). See internal/commands/msix.go and internal/commands/webview2/ for the full workflow. There is no internal/commands/packager.go and no internal/commands/windows_resources/ directory. Optional code-signing for the executable runs via wails3 tool sign (Authenticode) — see internal/commands/sign.go . 5. Customising the Pipeline Need Approach Extra build tags wails3 build --tags myFeature,otherTag Linter / pre-build step Add a task to build/Taskfile.yml and make the OS-specific build task depend on it Cross-compile Run the relevant OS task (e.g. wails3 task linux:build ) — there is no -platform flag Skip packaging Just run the build task; package is separate Custom packager Drop a config under internal/commands/myapp.* and call wails3 tool package with -config <file> Strip symbols Edit the darwin:/windows:/linux: build task to pass -ldflags "-s -w" directly to go build — wails3 build itself has no -ldflags flag All Taskfile targets respect the env vars Wails publishes ( APP_NAME , WAILS_VITE_PORT , FRONTEND_DEVSERVER_URL , …) so custom tasks can rely on them. 6. Troubleshooting Symptom Likely Cause Fix ld: framework not found WebKit (mac) Xcode CLI tools missing xcode-select --install Blank window in prod build Frontend build failed or SPA routing Check frontend/dist/index.html exists and your asset handler falls back to it MSIX packaging tools missing WebView2 SDK / MSIX tools not installed Run wails3 task install:msix:tools linuxdeploy not found Plugin missing on PATH Install linuxdeploy + run internal/commands/linuxdeploy-plugin-gtk.sh via the CLI’s auto-install step wails3 build has no -verbose flag. Set TASK_X_VERBOSE=1 (Taskfile) or inspect the task target directly to see the commands being executed. 7. Key Source Map Concern File Build wrapper internal/commands/task_wrapper.go ( Build , Package , SignWrapper , wrapTask ) Build-asset generation internal/commands/build-assets.go ( GenerateBuildAssets , UpdateBuildAssets ) Build info printer internal/commands/tool_buildinfo.go AppImage builder internal/commands/appimage.go Linux packaging (nfpm) internal/packager/packager.go , internal/commands/myapp.{DEB,RPM,ARCHLINUX} Windows MSIX internal/commands/msix.go , internal/commands/webview2/ Windows resource generator internal/commands/syso.go macOS DMG assets internal/commands/dmg/ .desktop generator internal/commands/dot_desktop.go Version constants internal/version/version.go Keep this table handy when you trace a build failure. You now have the full picture from source code to installer . The TL;DR is that wails3 build itself is a thin wrapper — almost every customisation happens in the project’s Taskfile.yml / build/config.yml , or via the explicit wails3 generate … / wails3 tool … subcommands. Happy shipping!

title: Codebase Layout
description: How the Wails v3 repository is organised and how the pieces fit together
text: Wails v3 lives in a monorepo that contains the framework runtime, CLI, examples, documentation, and build tool-chain. This page walks through the directory structure that matters to anyone digging into the internals. Top-Level View text Copy wails/ ├── v3/ # ⬅️ Everything specific to Wails v3 lives here ├── v2/ # Legacy v2 implementation (can be ignored for v3 work) ├── docs/ # Astro-powered v3 docs site (this page!) ├── website/ # Docusaurus v2 site and marketing pages (main site) ├── scripts/ # Misc helper scripts (e.g. sponsor image generator) └── *.md # Project-wide meta files (CHANGELOG, LICENSE, …) From here on, we zoom into the v3/ tree. v3/ Root text Copy v3/ ├── cmd/ # Compilable commands (currently only the wails3 CLI) ├── internal/ # Framework implementation (not public API) ├── pkg/ # Public Go packages — the API surface ├── tasks/ # Taskfile-based release / generation utilities ├── wep/ # RFC-style proposals (Wails Enhancement Proposals) ├── tests/ # Integration test harness ├── go.mod └── go.sum Project templates ship under internal/templates/ (one folder per framework stack plus base/ , _common/ , and ios/ ). There is no v3/templates/ directory at the top level. Mental Model pkg/ exposes what application developers import internal/ contains how the magic is implemented cmd/wails3 drives project lifecycle & builds Everything else supports those three pillars. cmd/ – Commands Path Notes v3/cmd/wails3 The CLI entrypoint . A tiny main.go delegates all logic to packages in internal/commands . internal/commands/* Sub-commands (init, dev, build, doctor, …). Each lives in its own file for easy discoverability. internal/commands/task_wrapper.go Bridges between CLI flags and the Taskfile build pipeline. The CLI owns: Project scaffolding ( init , template generation) Dev server orchestration ( dev , live-reload) Production builds & packaging ( build , package , platform wrappers) Diagnostics ( doctor ) internal/ – The Engine Room text Copy internal/ ├── assetserver/ # Serving & embedding web assets ├── buildinfo/ # Reproducible build metadata ├── commands/ # CLI mechanics (see above) ├── runtime/ # Build-tag glue + embedded JS runtime sources ├── generator/ # Static analysis & binding generator ├── templates/ # Project templates (frontend stacks) ├── packager/ # nfpm wrapper used by `wails3 tool package` ├── capabilities/ # Host OS capability probing ├── dbus/ # Generic D-Bus helper ├── service/ # Service-template scaffolding (`wails3 generate service`) └── ... # [other helper sub-packages: flags, hash, term, …] Key Sub-Packages Package Responsibility Where It Connects runtime Houses the small runtime{,_darwin,_linux,_windows,_android,_dev,_prod}.go build-tag glue plus the embedded JS runtime under runtime/desktop/ . The actual per-OS window/clipboard/dialog/tray code lives in pkg/application/*_{darwin,linux,windows}.go . Imported indirectly via pkg/application . assetserver Dual-mode file server: • Dev: serves from disk & proxies Vite ( build_dev.go ) • Prod: embeds assets via go:embed ( build_production.go ) Initialized by pkg/application during startup. generator Parses Go source to build binding metadata which later produces TypeScript/JS stub files and event constants. Entry points: generator.Generate / generator.Generator over collect/ + render/ . Triggered by wails3 generate bindings . packager nfpm wrapper used to emit Linux deb / rpm / archlinux artifacts (driven by myapp.DEB / .RPM / .ARCHLINUX nfpm configs under internal/commands/ ). Invoked by wails3 tool package . macOS DMG / Windows MSIX live under internal/commands/{dmg,msix.go,webview2/} . Supporting utilities (eg. s/ , hash/ , flags/ ) keep internal concerns decoupled. pkg/ – Public API text Copy pkg/ ├── application/ # Core API: App, windows, menus, dialogs, events, managers ├── events/ # Event constants (Common/Mac/Windows/Linux) + generator ├── services/ # Optional built-in services (notifications, kvstore, …) ├── doctor-ng/ # New-style `wails3 doctor-ng` checks ├── errs/ # Shared error types ├── icons/ # Default platform icons ├── mac/ # macOS-only helpers └── w32/ # Windows Win32 helpers There is no pkg/runtime/ , pkg/options/ or pkg/menu/ package. Window/menu options live alongside pkg/application (e.g. WebviewWindowOptions , Menu , MenuItem ), and assetserver/ is under internal/ . pkg/application bootstraps a Wails program: go Copy func main () { app := application. New (application. Options { Name : "MyApp" , Assets : application. AssetOptions { Handler : application. AssetFileServerFS (assetsFS), }, }) window := app. Window . New () window. SetTitle ( "Hello" ). SetSize ( 1024 , 768 ) _ = app. Run () } Under the hood it: Wires up the internal/runtime build-tag glue and per-OS code in pkg/application/ Sets up an internal/assetserver instance Registers any binding-driven message processors Enters the OS main thread internal/templates/ – Scaffolding Blueprints internal/templates/ ships base templates (Go layout under base/ , _common/ , ios/ ) and frontend skins ( vanilla[-ts] , react[-ts] , react-swc[-ts] , lit[-ts] , preact[-ts] , qwik[-ts] , solid[-ts] , svelte[-ts] , sveltekit[-ts] , vue[-ts] ). At wails3 init -t react , the CLI: Copies _common Go files Merges the desired frontend pack Runs go mod tidy (skippable with --skipgomodtidy ) Editing templates does not affect existing apps, only future init s. The public examples live under v3/examples/ ; they are not a substitute for the automated test suites described in the contributor documentation. tasks/ – Release Automation Taskfiles wrap complex cross-compilation, version bumping, and changelog generation. They are consumed programmatically by internal/commands/task.go so the same logic powers CLI and CI . How the Pieces Interact d2 Copy direction : down CLI : "wails3 CLI" Generator : "internal/generator" AssetDev : "assetserver (dev)" Packager : "internal/packager" AppRuntime : { label : "App runtime" ApplicationPkg : "pkg.application" InternalRuntime : "internal.runtime" OSAPIs : "OS APIs" } CLI -> Generator : "build / generate" CLI -> AssetDev : "dev" CLI -> Packager : "package" Generator -> ApplicationPkg : "bindings" ApplicationPkg -> InternalRuntime InternalRuntime -> OSAPIs ApplicationPkg -> AssetDev CLI → generator → runtime forms the core path from source to running desktop app . Orientation Tips Need to understand… Look at… Platform shims pkg/application/*_darwin.go , *_linux.go , *_windows.go (window, clipboard, dialogs, systray, mainthread, events_common). Linux cgo: pkg/application/linux_cgo*.go . Bridge protocol pkg/application/messageprocessor*.go Asset workflow internal/assetserver/ ( build_dev.go vs build_production.go ) Packaging flow internal/commands/{appimage,msix,dot_desktop,dmg/}.go , internal/packager/ Template engine internal/templates/ ( templates.Install , templates.GetDefaultTemplates ) Static analysis internal/generator/{generate.go,collect/,render/} You now have a mental map of the repository. Use it with ripgrep , your IDE’s “Go to File/Symbol”, and the example apps to navigate deeper into any feature. Happy hacking!

title: Extending Wails
description: Practical guide to adding new features and platforms to Wails v3
text: Wails is designed to be hackable . Every major subsystem lives in Go code you can read, modify, and ship. This page shows where to start and how to stay cross-platform when you: Add a Service (notifications, KV store, custom IPC, …) Create a new CLI command ( wails3 <foo> ) Extend the Runtime (window API, dialogs, events) Introduce a Platform capability (Wayland, …) Keep cross-platform compatibility without drowning in //go:build tags 1. Adding a Service A “service” in v3 is a user-supplied Go type that’s registered through application.Options.Services and exposed to JS via generated bindings. The v3 codebase ships: internal/service/ — scaffolding for wails3 generate service : text Copy internal/service/ ├── service.go # Install(options *flags.ServiceInit) └── template/ ├── README.tmpl.md ├── go.mod.tmpl ├── service.go.tmpl └── service.tmpl.yml pkg/services/ — ready-made services you can register today (notifications, kvstore, sqlite, log, fileserver, dock, …). The generator and CLI files referenced by older drafts as internal/service/template/template.go and internal/generator/collect/services.go don’t exist — the scaffolder is internal/service/service.go (entry point service.Install ), and binding metadata for services is collected in internal/generator/collect/service.go . 1.1 Define the Service go Copy package chat type Service struct { messages []string } func New () * Service { return & Service {} } func (s * Service ) Send (msg string) string { s.messages = append (s.messages, msg) return "ok" } 1.2 Implement the lifecycle interfaces (optional) A service may optionally satisfy these interfaces (from pkg/application ): go Copy func (s * Service ) ServiceStartup (ctx context. Context , options application. ServiceOptions ) error { return nil } func (s * Service ) ServiceShutdown () error { return nil } Important: ServiceShutdown takes no arguments . A method with the signature ServiceShutdown(ctx context.Context) error does not satisfy the interface and will silently never be called. 1.3 Register the service with the application There is no global services.Register(...) call. Services are registered at runtime via application.Options.Services : go Copy app := application. New (application. Options { Services : []application. Service { application. NewService (chat. New ()), }, }) Once registered, wails3 generate bindings emits ES modules under frontend/bindings/<your import path>/... that wrap the exported methods. 1.4 Calling from JS js Copy import { Send } from "../bindings/github.com/you/yourapp/chat" ; await Send ( "hi" ); There is no window.backend.* global in v3 — calls go through the generated ES modules, which in turn call Call.ByID(...) from /wails/runtime.js . 2. Writing a New CLI Command The v3 CLI uses github.com/leaanthony/clir (not cobra). Wiring lives in v3/cmd/wails3/main.go : go Copy import "github.com/leaanthony/clir" func main () { app := clir. NewCli ( "wails" , "The Wails3 CLI" , "v3" ) app. NewSubCommand ( "hello" , "Prints Hello Wails" ). Action ( func () error { fmt. Println ( "Hello Wails!" ) return nil }) // ... other subcommands explicitly wired here _ = app. Run () } There is no init() -based auto-registration. Add your new subcommand to cmd/wails3/main.go , plus a backing function in internal/commands/ (and a flag struct under internal/flags/ if it takes options). Re-build the CLI: text Copy cd v3 go install ./cmd/wails3 wails3 hello If your command needs the Taskfile glue, reuse helpers in internal/commands/task_wrapper.go ( wrapTask("yourtask", args) ). 3. Modifying the Runtime Common reasons: New window feature ( SetOpacity , Shake , …) Extra dialog ( ColorPicker ) System-level API (screen brightness) 3.1 Public API Add the method to pkg/application/webview_window.go (the interface lives in window.go ): go Copy func (w * WebviewWindow ) SetOpacity (o float32) Window { InvokeSync ( func () { w.impl. setOpacity (o) }) return w } Use the existing InvokeSync / InvokeAsync helpers to ensure the call runs on the main thread. 3.2 Message Processor If JS needs to invoke the new method, extend the appropriate pkg/application/messageprocessor_*.go file. The message processor uses switch-based methods on MessageProcessor , not a global register(...) call: go Copy // inside messageprocessor_window.go case "setOpacity" : var args struct { WindowID uint `json:"windowID"` Opacity float32 `json:"opacity"` } if err := json. Unmarshal (payload, & args); err != nil { ... } window, _ := m.app. Window . GetByID (args. WindowID ) window. SetOpacity (args. Opacity ) There is no messageprocessor_window_opacity.go file or init() -based register(MsgSetOpacity, ...) pattern in the codebase. 3.3 Platform Implementation Add the implementation to each per-OS file under pkg/application/ : text Copy pkg/application/ ├── webview_window_darwin.go //go:build darwin ├── webview_window_linux.go //go:build linux └── webview_window_windows.go //go:build windows If a platform can’t support the feature, write a no-op stub. The framework has no ErrCapability sentinel — surface support via documentation and, if needed, via the relevant boolean field on Options / the platform-specific options struct. 3.4 Capability Flag (optional) The internal/capabilities/ package exists for declaring per-platform capability sets. There is no public application.HasCapability / application.CapOpacity API. If you want a runtime-checkable capability, add it under internal/capabilities/ and surface a typed getter from pkg/application . 4. Adding New Platform Capabilities Example: optional Wayland support on Linux. Split the relevant pkg/application/*_linux.go file into *_linux_x11.go ( //go:build linux && !wayland ) and *_linux_wayland.go ( //go:build linux && wayland ). Have users opt in with wails3 build --tags wayland . Forward extra tags through the existing EXTRA_TAGS plumbing in internal/commands/task_wrapper.go . There is no dev -level --tags wayland flag — wails3 dev accepts only --config , --port , and -s . Update docs and any platform-specific README under pkg/application/ . Keep default build tags minimal; reserve opt-in tags for niche features. 5. Cross-Platform Compatibility Checklist ✅ Step Why Provide every public method in all platform files (even if stub) Keeps the build green on every OS Document graceful degradation per OS Apps can branch on runtime.GOOS without hidden errors Use pure Go first, Cgo only when needed Simplifies cross-compiles (Linux already pays the Cgo tax) Run task test:cli , task test:generator , task test:templates Reproduces CI locally Document new build tags in the contributor docs / template README Users must know about opt-ins 6. Debug Builds & Iteration Speed Use Options.LogLevel = slog.LevelDebug ( Options.Logger = slog.Default() ) to print verbose runtime activity. There is no WAILS_LOG_LEVEL environment variable. wails3 dev flags are --config , --port , -s . There is no -race or -verbose flag — exercise the race detector with go test -race ./... or by go build -race -ing your app and running it directly. The race / Cgo testing guide lives in v3/TESTING.md (older drafts pointed at pkg/application/RACE.md , which doesn’t exist). 7. Upstream Contributions For new functionality or a public behaviour change, open a draft WEP (Wails Enhancement Proposal) PR to discuss the idea and design. Use an issue only for a reproducible bug or a documentation problem. Follow the techniques above to implement. Add: Unit tests ( *_test.go ) Documentation (this file or the relevant docs/... page) A regression test under internal/generator/testcases/ if you touched the bindings generator Run task precommit plus the relevant task test:* targets locally before pushing. Quick Links Area Location Built-in services pkg/services/ Service scaffolder internal/service/ CLI wiring v3/cmd/wails3/main.go CLI command bodies internal/commands/ Per-OS runtime pkg/application/*_{darwin,linux,windows}.go Capability declarations internal/capabilities/ Taskfile DSL v3/Taskfile.yaml Event-constants generator v3/tasks/events/generate.go You now have a roadmap for bending Wails to your will — add services, sprinkle CLI magic, hack the runtime, or bring entirely new OS features. Happy extending!

title: Getting Started
description: How to start contributing to Wails v3
text: Welcome, Contributor! Thank you for your interest in contributing to Wails! This guide will help you make your first contribution. Prerequisites Before you begin, ensure you have: Go 1.25+ installed ( download ) Node.js 20+ and npm ( download ) Git configured with your GitHub account Basic familiarity with Go and JavaScript/TypeScript Platform-Specific Requirements macOS: Xcode Command Line Tools: xcode-select --install Windows: MSYS2 or similar Unix-like environment recommended WebView2 runtime (usually pre-installed on Windows 11) Linux: gcc , pkg-config , libgtk-4-dev , libwebkitgtk-6.0-dev (default GTK4 stack) Install via: sudo apt install build-essential pkg-config libgtk-4-dev libwebkitgtk-6.0-dev (Debian/Ubuntu) For the legacy -tags gtk3 build path, also install libgtk-3-dev and libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev Contribution Process Overview The typical contribution workflow follows these steps: Fork & Clone - Create your own copy of the Wails repository Setup - Build the Wails CLI and verify your environment Branch - Create a feature branch for your changes Develop - Make your changes following our coding standards Test - Run tests to ensure everything works Commit - Commit with clear, conventional commit messages Submit - Open a pull request for review Iterate - Respond to feedback and make adjustments Merge - Once approved, your changes become part of Wails! Step-by-Step Guide Choose your contribution type: Bug Fix WEP (Enhancement) Documentation 1 Find or Report the Bug Check if the bug is already reported in GitHub Issues If not, create a new issue with steps to reproduce Wait for confirmation before starting work 2 Fork and Clone Fork the repository at github.com/wailsapp/wails/fork Clone your fork: bash Copy git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/wails.git cd wails git remote add upstream https://github.com/wailsapp/wails.git 3 Build and Verify Build Wails and verify you can reproduce the bug: bash Copy cd v3 go build -o ../wails3 ./cmd/wails3 # Reproduce the bug to understand it 4 Create a Bug Fix Branch Create a branch for your fix: bash Copy git checkout -b fix/issue-123-window-crash 5 Fix the Bug Make the minimal changes needed to fix the bug Don’t refactor unrelated code Add or update tests to prevent regression bash Copy # Make your changes # Add tests in *_test.go files 6 Test Your Fix Run tests to ensure the fix works: bash Copy go test ./... # Test the specific package go test ./pkg/application -v # Run with race detector go test ./... -race 7 Commit Your Fix Commit with a clear message: bash Copy git commit -m "fix: prevent window crash when closing during initialization Fixes #123" 8 Submit Pull Request Push and create PR: bash Copy git push origin fix/issue-123-window-crash In your PR description: Explain the bug and root cause Describe your fix Reference the issue: “Fixes #123” Include before/after behavior 9 Respond to Feedback Address review comments and update your PR as needed. 1 Write a WEP Read the WEP (Wails Enhancement Proposal) process Copy the WEP template into v3/wep/proposals/<name>/proposal.md Open a draft PR titled [WEP] <title> containing the WEP only Wait for a maintainer decision before implementing 2 Fork and Clone Fork the repository at github.com/wailsapp/wails/fork Clone your fork: bash Copy git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/wails.git cd wails git remote add upstream https://github.com/wailsapp/wails.git 3 Setup Development Environment Build Wails and verify your environment: bash Copy cd v3 go build -o ../wails3 ./cmd/wails3 # Run tests to ensure everything works go test ./... 4 Create a Feature Branch Create a descriptive branch: bash Copy git checkout -b feat/window-transparency-support 5 Implement the Feature Follow our Coding Standards Keep changes focused on the feature Write clean, documented code Add comprehensive tests bash Copy # Example: Adding a new window method # 1. Add to window.go interface # 2. Implement in platform files (darwin, windows, linux) # 3. Add tests # 4. Update documentation 6 Test Thoroughly Test your feature: bash Copy # Unit tests go test ./pkg/application -v # Integration test - create a test app cd .. ./wails3 init -n feature-test cd feature-test # Add code using your new feature ../wails3 dev 7 Document Your Feature Add docstrings to all public APIs Update relevant documentation in /docs/src/content/docs/ Add examples if applicable 8 Commit with Convention Use conventional commits: bash Copy git commit -m "feat: add window transparency support - Add SetTransparent() method to Window API - Implement for macOS, Windows, and Linux - Add tests and documentation Closes #456" 9 Submit Pull Request Push and create PR: bash Copy git push origin feat/window-transparency-support In your PR: Describe the feature and use cases Show examples or screenshots List any breaking changes Reference the accepted WEP PR 10 Iterate Based on Review Maintainers may request changes. Be patient and collaborative. 1 Identify Documentation Needs Found outdated docs while using Wails? Notice missing examples or explanations? Want to fix typos or improve clarity? Check documentation issues 2 Fork and Clone Fork the repository at github.com/wailsapp/wails/fork Clone your fork: bash Copy git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/wails.git cd wails git remote add upstream https://github.com/wailsapp/wails.git 3 Setup Documentation Environment The docs are in /docs/src/content/docs/ and built with Astro: bash Copy cd docs npm install npm run dev Open http://localhost:4321/ to preview changes live. 4 Create a Documentation Branch Create a branch for your changes: bash Copy git checkout -b docs/improve-window-api-examples 5 Make Your Changes Documentation files are in /docs/src/content/docs/ : bash Copy # Edit MDX files # Check the preview in your browser # Ensure formatting is correct Best Practices: Use clear, concise language Include practical code examples Add links to related sections Check spelling and grammar Test all code examples 6 Verify Your Changes Check the live preview and ensure: Links work correctly Code examples are accurate Formatting renders properly No broken images or references 7 Commit Documentation Changes Commit with clear message: bash Copy git commit -m "docs: add practical examples to Window API guide - Add window positioning examples - Include common patterns section - Fix broken links to Event API" 8 Submit Pull Request Push and create PR: bash Copy git push origin docs/improve-window-api-examples In your PR: Describe what docs you improved Explain why the change helps users Include screenshots if visual changes 9 Address Review Feedback Documentation PRs are usually quick to review and merge! Finding Issues to Work On Look for good first issue labels Check help wanted issues Browse open issues and ask to be assigned Getting Help Discord: Join Wails Discord Discussions: Post in GitHub Discussions Issues: Open an issue for a reproducible bug; use Discussions for questions and a WEP PR for enhancements Code of Conduct Be respectful, constructive, and welcoming. We’re building a friendly community focused on creating great software together. Next Steps Set up your Development Environment Review our Coding Standards Explore the Technical Documentation

title: Maintainer Triage
description: Triage bugs, documentation reports, and WEPs consistently
text: Purpose Issues record reproducible bugs and documentation problems. A WEP (Wails Enhancement Proposal) pull request records a proposed capability or change to public behaviour. Issue triage Confirm that a bug report includes a released version, platform, reproducible steps, expected behaviour, actual behaviour, and wails3 doctor output. Label confirmed reports Bug and apply the relevant version and platform labels. Ask for a minimal reproduction when needed. Keep documentation reports open when they identify a concrete documentation defect; encourage a PR when the reporter can make the change. Redirect feature requests to the WEP guide, then close them. The automated redirect workflow handles newly labelled enhancement issues; use the same wording for older issues. Move questions and support requests to GitHub Discussions or Discord. WEP triage Check that the PR is a draft titled [WEP] <title> and contains only the WEP and supporting material. Check that it uses the WEP template, identifies an implementor, and covers compatibility, platforms, testing, maintenance, and security/privacy. Keep technical discussion on the WEP PR. Discussions are useful context but are not the decision record. Record the maintainer decision in a PR comment: accepted, rejected, or withdrawn, with a short rationale. For an accepted WEP, assign its number, update the WEP index, merge the WEP PR, and require implementation PRs to link back to it. Existing enhancement issues Do not silently delete historical enhancement issues. For each still-relevant request, leave the redirect comment and close it; interested contributors can open a WEP. Close duplicates with a link to the existing WEP or decision.

title: Runtime Internals
description: Deep-dive into how Wails v3 boots, runs, and talks to the OS
text: The runtime is the layer that transforms ordinary Go functions into a cross-platform desktop application. This document explains the moving parts you will meet when tracing through the source code. 1. Application Lifecycle Phase Code Path What Happens Bootstrap pkg/application/application.go:init() Registers build-time data, creates a global application singleton. New() application.New(...) Validates Options , spins up the AssetServer , initialises logging. Run() application.(*App).Run() 1. Calls platform mainthread.X() to enter the OS UI thread. 2. Boots the runtime ( internal/runtime ). 3. Blocks until the last window closes or Quit() is called. Shutdown application.(*App).Quit() Broadcasts application:shutdown event, flushes log, tears down windows & services. The lifecycle is strictly single-entry : you may create many windows, but the application object itself is initialised once. 2. Window Management Public API go Copy win := app. Window . NewWithOptions (application. WebviewWindowOptions { Title : "Dashboard" , Width : 1280 , Height : 720 , }) win. Show () app.Window.New() takes no arguments ; use NewWithOptions(...) when you need to pass an application.WebviewWindowOptions struct (by value). app.Window.New[WithOptions]() delegates to pkg/application/webview_window_*.go where the platform-specific implementations live: text Copy pkg/application/ ├── webview_window_darwin.go // WKWebView ├── webview_window_linux.go // GTK + WebKitGTK (plus linux_cgo*.go) └── webview_window_windows.go // WebView2 Each file: Creates a native webview (WKWebView, WebKitGTK, WebView2). Registers a Message Processor callback ( pkg/application/messageprocessor*.go ). Maps Wails events ( WindowDidResize , WindowFocus , WindowFilesDropped , …) to the constants in pkg/events . internal/runtime/ is reserved for the small build-tag glue ( runtime{,_darwin,_linux,_windows,_android,_dev,_prod}.go ) and the embedded JS runtime under internal/runtime/desktop/ . Active windows are tracked by pkg/application/window_manager.go / webview_window.go . pkg/application/screenmanager.go is for display metadata (resolution, scale, work area) — it does not manage windows. 3. Message Processing Pipeline The bridge between JavaScript and Go is implemented by the Message Processor family in pkg/application/messageprocessor_*.go . Flow: JavaScript calls Call.ByID(<fnv-id>, ...args) from /wails/runtime.js (implemented in internal/runtime/desktop/@wailsio/runtime/src/calls.ts ) — or Call.ByName("pkg.Struct.Method", ...args) for name-mode builds. The runtime helper packages the call and dispatches it through the per-platform native bridge into Go. Go receives the message in pkg/application/messageprocessor_call.go . The processor looks up the bound method in pkg/application/bindings.go (hand-written, reflect -based) and invokes it. The result or error is marshalled back to JS where a Promise resolves or rejects. The exact JSON envelope is defined by the runtime helper on the JS side and by messageprocessor_call.go on the Go side — older drafts of this page quoted a {"t":"c","id":"123","m":"Greet","p":[…]} shape, but that doesn’t match the current implementation. Read both files together when chasing a wire-format bug. Specialised processors: File Purpose messageprocessor_window.go Window actions (hide, maximize, …) messageprocessor_dialog.go Native dialogs ( OpenFile , MessageBox , …) messageprocessor_clipboard.go Clipboard read/write messageprocessor_events.go Event subscribe / emit messageprocessor_browser.go Browser navigation, devtools Processors are stateless – they pull everything they need from the ApplicationContext passed with each message. 4. Events System Events are namespaced strings dispatched across three layers: Application events : global lifecycle ( application:ready , application:shutdown ). Window events : per-window ( window:focus , window:resize ). Custom events : user-defined ( chat:new-message ). Implementation details: Event constants live in pkg/events/ ( defaults.go , known_events.go , events.txt ). They are generated by v3/tasks/events/generate.go and exposed as events.Common.* , events.Mac.* , events.Windows.* , events.Linux.* . You can rebuild them with wails3 generate constants . Go side (application events): go Copy app. Event . OnApplicationEvent (events. Common . ApplicationStarted , func (e * application. ApplicationEvent ) {}) Go side (window events): go Copy window. OnWindowEvent (events. Common . WindowFocus , func (e * application. WindowEvent ) {}) Go side (custom events): go Copy app. Event . On ( "chat:new-message" , func (e * application. CustomEvent ) {}) JS side: js Copy import { Events } from "/wails/runtime.js" ; Events . On ( "chat:new-message" , (e) => { / * … * / }); Application/window/custom events all flow through pkg/application/event_manager.go . Window-event subscriptions are scoped to their window, so closing the window unregisters its handlers automatically. 5. Platform-Specific Implementations Conditional compilation keeps the public API identical while hiding OS wrinkles. Concern Darwin Linux Windows Main Thread mainthread_darwin.go (Cgo to Foundation) mainthread_linux.go (GTK) mainthread_windows.go (Win32 AttachThreadInput ) Dialogs dialogs_darwin.* (NSAlert) dialogs_linux.go (GtkFileChooser) dialogs_windows.go (IFileOpenDialog) Clipboard clipboard_darwin.go clipboard_linux.go clipboard_windows.go Tray Icons systemtray_darwin.* systemtray_linux.go (DBus) systemtray_windows.go (Shell_NotifyIcon) Key principles: macOS and Windows use Cgo sparingly (mostly through pkg/mac/ and the w32 Win32 wrappers in pkg/w32 ). Linux is heavily Cgo by necessity — pkg/application/linux_cgo.go (~69 KB) plus linux_cgo_gtk4.{c,go,h} (~50 KB+) drive GTK/WebKitGTK directly. Use build tags ( //go:build darwin , //go:build linux , …) to keep per-OS files readable. internal/capabilities/ exists for per-platform capability flags, but the framework does not export an ErrCapability sentinel — feature gating is done by platform-specific stub returns. 6. File Guide File Why You’d Touch It internal/runtime/runtime_*.go Change the small build-tag stub layer (dev vs prod, OS-specific glue). pkg/application/webview_window_*.go Implement a new window hint or behaviour. pkg/application/messageprocessor*.go Add a new bridge command callable from JS. pkg/events/*.go Extend built-in event definitions (then re-run wails3 generate constants ). internal/assetserver/* Tweak dev/production asset handling. internal/runtime/desktop/@wailsio/runtime/src/* Edit the embedded JS runtime (call/event dispatch, dialogs, drag, …). 7. Debugging Tips Configure Options.LogLevel (e.g. slog.LevelDebug ) and inspect Options.Logger output — there is no WAILS_LOG_LEVEL environment variable. wails3 dev flags are --config , --port , -s (enable HTTPS) and the global --no-colour . There is no -verbose flag. On macOS run under lldb -- to catch Objective-C exceptions early. For Windows Chromium issues, enable WebView2 debug logs: set WEBVIEW2_ADDITIONAL_BROWSER_ARGUMENTS=--remote-debugging-port=9222 8. Extending the Runtime Optional: declare any new capability flag in internal/capabilities/ . Implement the feature in each pkg/application/*_{darwin,linux,windows}.go variant using build tags. Provide a stub on platforms that don’t support it. Add the public API in pkg/application (interface + concrete WebviewWindow methods, options struct, etc.). Register a new message-processor method ( pkg/application/messageprocessor*.go ) and a matching helper in the JS runtime if JS needs to call it. If you add an event, declare its constant in pkg/events/ and run wails3 generate constants to refresh the generated files. Follow this checklist and you’ll keep the cross-platform contract intact. 9. Drag-and-Drop File drag-and-drop uses a JavaScript-first approach on all platforms. The native layer intercepts OS drag events, but the actual drop handling and DOM interaction happens in JavaScript. Flow User drags files from OS over the Wails window Native layer detects the drag and notifies JavaScript for hover effects User drops files Native layer sends file paths + coordinates to JavaScript JavaScript finds the drop target element ( data-file-drop-target ) JavaScript sends file paths + element details to Go backend Go emits WindowFilesDropped event with full context Platform Implementations Platform Native Layer Key Challenge Windows WebView2’s built-in drag support Coordinates in CSS pixels, no conversion needed macOS NSWindow drag delegates Convert window-relative to webview-relative coords Linux GTK3 drag signals Must distinguish file drags from internal HTML5 drags Linux: Distinguishing Drag Types GTK and WebKit both want to handle drag events. The key is checking the drag target type: c Copy static gboolean is_file_drag ( GdkDragContext * context) { GList * targets = gdk_drag_context_list_targets (context); for ( GList * l = targets; l != NULL ; l = l -> next) { GdkAtom atom = GDK_POINTER_TO_ATOM (l -> data); gchar * name = gdk_atom_name (atom); if (name && g_strcmp0 (name, "text/uri-list" ) == 0 ) { g_free (name); return TRUE ; // External file drag } g_free (name); } return FALSE ; // Internal HTML5 drag } Signal handlers return FALSE for internal drags (letting WebKit handle them) and TRUE for file drags (handling them ourselves). Blocking File Drops When EnableFileDrop is false , we still need to prevent the browser from navigating to dropped files. Each platform handles this differently: Windows : JavaScript calls preventDefault() on drag events macOS : JavaScript calls preventDefault() on drag events Linux : GTK signal handlers intercept and reject file drags at the native level Key Files File Purpose pkg/application/linux_cgo.go GTK drag signal handlers (C code in cgo preamble) pkg/application/webview_window_darwin.go macOS drag delegates pkg/application/webview_window_windows.go WebView2 message handling internal/runtime/desktop/@wailsio/runtime/src/window.ts JavaScript drop handling Debugging Linux : Add printf in C code (remember fflush(stdout) ) Windows : Use globalApplication.debug() JavaScript : Check browser console, enable debug mode Common issues: Internal HTML5 drag not working : Native handler intercepting it (return FALSE for non-file drags) Hover effects not showing : JavaScript handlers not being called Wrong coordinates : Check coordinate space conversions You now have a guided tour of the runtime internals. Combine this knowledge with the Codebase Layout map and the Asset Server docs to navigate confidently and make impactful contributions. Happy coding!

title: Development Setup
description: Set up your development environment for Wails v3 development
text: Development Environment Setup This guide walks you through setting up a complete development environment for working on Wails v3. Required Tools Go Development Install Go 1.25 or later: bash Copy # Download from https://go.dev/dl/ go version # Verify installation Configure Go environment: bash Copy # Add to your shell profile (.bashrc, .zshrc, etc.) export GOPATH=$HOME/go export PATH=$PATH:$GOPATH/bin Install useful Go tools: bash Copy go install golang.org/x/tools/cmd/goimports@latest go install github.com/golangci/golangci-lint/cmd/golangci-lint@latest Node.js and npm Required for building documentation and testing frontend integrations. bash Copy # Install Node.js 20+ and npm node --version # Should be 20+ npm --version Platform-Specific Dependencies macOS: bash Copy # Install Xcode Command Line Tools xcode-select --install # Verify installation xcode-select -p # Should output a path Windows: Install MSYS2 for a Unix-like environment WebView2 Runtime (pre-installed on Windows 11, download for Windows 10) Optional: Install Git for Windows Linux (Debian/Ubuntu): bash Copy sudo apt update # Default GTK4 + WebKitGTK 6.0 stack (Ubuntu 24.04+ / Debian 13+) sudo apt install build-essential pkg-config libgtk-4-dev libwebkitgtk-6.0-dev # For the legacy -tags gtk3 path: sudo apt install libgtk-3-dev libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev Linux (Fedora/RHEL): bash Copy # Default GTK4 stack sudo dnf install gcc pkg-config gtk4-devel webkitgtk6.0-devel # Legacy GTK3 path: sudo dnf install gtk3-devel webkit2gtk4.1-devel Linux (Arch): bash Copy # Default GTK4 stack sudo pacman -S base-devel gtk4 webkitgtk-6.0 # Legacy GTK3 path: sudo pacman -S gtk3 webkit2gtk-4.1 Repository Setup Clone and Configure bash Copy # Clone your fork git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/wails.git cd wails # Add upstream remote git remote add upstream https://github.com/wailsapp/wails.git # Verify remotes git remote -v Build the Wails CLI bash Copy # Navigate to v3 directory cd v3 # Build the CLI go build -o ../wails3 ./cmd/wails3 # Test the build cd .. ./wails3 version Add to PATH (Optional) Linux/macOS: bash Copy # Add to ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc export PATH=$PATH:/path/to/wails Windows: Add the Wails directory to your PATH environment variable through System Properties. IDE Setup VS Code (Recommended) Install VS Code: Download Install extensions: Go (by Go Team at Google) ESLint Prettier MDX (for documentation) Configure workspace settings ( .vscode/settings.json ): json Copy { "go.useLanguageServer" : true , "go.lintTool" : "golangci-lint" , "go.lintOnSave" : "workspace" , "editor.formatOnSave" : true , "go.formatTool" : "goimports" } GoLand Install GoLand: Download Configure: Enable Go modules support Set up file watchers for goimports Configure code style to match project conventions Verify Your Setup Run these commands to verify everything is working: bash Copy # Go version check go version # Build Wails cd v3 go build ./cmd/wails3 # Run tests go test ./pkg/... # Create a test app cd .. ./wails3 init -n mytest -t vanilla cd mytest ../wails3 dev If the test app builds and runs, your environment is ready! Running Tests Unit Tests bash Copy cd v3 go test ./... Specific Package Tests bash Copy go test ./pkg/application go test ./pkg/events -v # Verbose output Run with Coverage bash Copy go test ./... -coverprofile=coverage.out go tool cover -html=coverage.out Run with Race Detector bash Copy go test ./... -race Working with Documentation The Wails documentation is built with Astro and Starlight. bash Copy cd docs # Install dependencies npm install # Start dev server npm run dev # Build for production npm run build Documentation will be available at http://localhost:4321/ Debugging Debugging Go Code VS Code: Create .vscode/launch.json : json Copy { "version" : "0.2.0" , "configurations" : [ { "name" : "Debug Wails CLI" , "type" : "go" , "request" : "launch" , "mode" : "debug" , "program" : "${workspaceFolder}/v3/cmd/wails3" , "args" : [ "dev" ] } ] } Command Line: bash Copy # Use Delve debugger go install github.com/go-delve/delve/cmd/dlv@latest dlv debug ./cmd/wails3 -- dev Debugging Platform Code Platform-specific debugging requires platform tools: macOS: Xcode Instruments Windows: Visual Studio Debugger Linux: GDB Common Issues “command not found: wails3” Add the Wails directory to your PATH or use ./wails3 from the project root. “webkitgtk-6.0 not found” or “webkit2gtk not found” (Linux) Install the development packages for whichever stack you’re building against: bash Copy # Default GTK4 stack (Debian/Ubuntu): sudo apt install libwebkitgtk-6.0-dev # Legacy GTK3 path: sudo apt install libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev Build fails with Go module errors bash Copy cd v3 go mod tidy go mod download “CGO_ENABLED” errors on Windows Ensure you have a C compiler (MinGW-w64 via MSYS2) in your PATH. Next Steps Review Coding Standards Explore the Technical Documentation Find an issue to work on: Good First Issues

title: Coding Standards
description: Code style, conventions, and best practices for Wails v3
text: Code Style and Conventions Following consistent coding standards makes the codebase easier to read, maintain, and contribute to. Go Code Standards Code Formatting Use standard Go formatting tools: bash Copy # Format all code gofmt -w . # Use goimports for import organization goimports -w . Required: All Go code must pass gofmt and goimports before committing. Naming Conventions Packages: Lowercase, single word when possible package application , package events Avoid underscores or mixed caps Exported Names: PascalCase for types, functions, constants type WebviewWindow struct , func NewApplication() Unexported Names: camelCase for internal types, functions, variables type windowImpl struct , func createWindow() Interfaces: Name by behavior: Reader , Writer , Handler Single-method interfaces: name with -er suffix go Copy // Good type Closer interface { Close () error } // Avoid type CloseInterface interface { Close () error } Error Handling Always check errors: go Copy // Good result, err := doSomething () if err != nil { return fmt. Errorf ( "failed to do something: %w" , err) } // Bad - ignoring errors result, _ := doSomething () Use error wrapping: go Copy // Wrap errors to provide context if err := validate (); err != nil { return fmt. Errorf ( "validation failed: %w" , err) } Create custom error types when needed: go Copy type ValidationError struct { Field string Value string } func (e * ValidationError ) Error () string { return fmt. Sprintf ( "invalid value %q for field %q" , e. Value , e. Field ) } Comments and Documentation Package comments: go Copy // Package application provides the core Wails application runtime. // // It handles window management, event dispatching, and service lifecycle. package application Exported declarations: go Copy // NewApplication creates a new Wails application with the given options. // // The application must be started with Run() or RunWithContext(). func NewApplication (opts Options ) * Application { // ... } Implementation comments: go Copy // processEvent handles incoming events from the runtime. // It dispatches to registered handlers and manages event lifecycle. func (a * Application ) processEvent (event * Event ) { // Validate event before processing if event == nil { return } // Find and invoke handlers // ... } Function and Method Structure Keep functions focused: go Copy // Good - single responsibility func (w * Window ) setTitle (title string) { w.title = title w. updateNativeTitle () } // Bad - doing too much func (w * Window ) updateEverything () { w. setTitle (w.title) w. setSize (w.width, w.height) w. setPosition (w.x, w.y) // ... 20 more operations } Use early returns: go Copy // Good func validate (input string) error { if input == "" { return errors. New ( "empty input" ) } if len (input) > 100 { return errors. New ( "input too long" ) } return nil } // Avoid deep nesting Concurrency Use context for cancellation: go Copy func (a * Application ) RunWithContext (ctx context. Context ) error { select { case <- ctx. Done () : return ctx. Err () case <- a.done : return nil } } Protect shared state with mutexes: go Copy type SafeCounter struct { mu sync. Mutex count int } func (c * SafeCounter ) Increment () { c.mu. Lock () defer c.mu. Unlock () c.count ++ } Avoid goroutine leaks: go Copy // Good - goroutine has exit condition func (a * Application ) startWorker (ctx context. Context ) { go func () { for { select { case <- ctx. Done () : return // Clean exit case work := <- a.workChan : a. process (work) } } }() } Testing Test file naming: go Copy // Implementation: window.go // Tests: window_test.go Table-driven tests: go Copy func TestValidate (t * testing. T ) { tests := [] struct { name string input string wantErr bool }{ { "empty input" , "" , true }, { "valid input" , "hello" , false }, { "too long" , strings. Repeat ( "a" , 101 ), true }, } for _, tt := range tests { t. Run (tt.name, func (t * testing. T ) { err := validate (tt.input) if (err != nil ) != tt.wantErr { t. Errorf ( "validate() error = %v, wantErr %v" , err, tt.wantErr) } }) } } JavaScript/TypeScript Standards Code Formatting Use Prettier for consistent formatting: json Copy { "semi" : false , "singleQuote" : true , "tabWidth" : 2 , "trailingComma" : "es5" } Naming Conventions Variables and functions: camelCase: const userName = "John" Classes and types: PascalCase: class WindowManager Constants: UPPER SNAKE CASE: const MAX_RETRIES = 3 TypeScript Use explicit types: typescript Copy // Good function greet (name : string) : string { return `Hello, ${name}` } // Avoid implicit any function process (data) { // Bad return data } Define interfaces: typescript Copy interface WindowOptions { title : string width : number height : number } function createWindow (options : WindowOptions ) : void { // ... } Commit Message Format Use Conventional Commits : text Copy <type>(<scope>): <subject> <body> <footer> Types: feat : New feature fix : Bug fix docs : Documentation changes refactor : Code refactoring test : Adding or updating tests chore : Maintenance tasks Examples: text Copy feat(window): add SetAlwaysOnTop method Implement SetAlwaysOnTop for keeping windows above others. Adds platform implementations for macOS, Windows, and Linux. Closes #123 text Copy fix(events): prevent event handler memory leak Event listeners were not being properly cleaned up when windows were closed. This adds explicit cleanup in the window destructor. Pull Request Guidelines Before Submitting Code passes gofmt and goimports All tests pass ( go test ./... ) New code has tests Documentation updated if needed Commit messages follow conventions No merge conflicts with master PR Description Template markdown Copy ## Description Brief description of what this PR does. ## Type of Change - [ ] Bug fix - [ ] New feature - [ ] Breaking change - [ ] Documentation update ## Testing How was this tested? ## Checklist - [ ] Tests pass - [ ] Documentation updated - [ ] No breaking changes (or documented) Code Review Process As a Reviewer Be constructive and respectful Focus on code quality, not personal preferences Explain why changes are suggested Approve once satisfied As an Author Respond to all comments Ask for clarification if needed Make requested changes or explain why not Be open to feedback Best Practices Performance Avoid premature optimization Profile before optimizing Use benchmarks for performance-critical code go Copy func BenchmarkProcess (b * testing. B ) { for i := 0 ; i < b. N ; i ++ { process (testData) } } Security Validate all user input Sanitize data before display Use crypto/rand for random data Never log sensitive information Documentation Document exported APIs Include examples in documentation Update docs when changing APIs Keep README files current Platform-Specific Code File Naming text Copy window.go // Common interface window_darwin.go // macOS implementation window_windows.go // Windows implementation window_linux.go // Linux implementation Build Tags go Copy //go:build darwin package application // macOS-specific code Linting Run linters before committing: bash Copy # golangci-lint (recommended) golangci-lint run # Individual linters go vet ./... staticcheck ./... Questions? If you’re unsure about any standards: Check existing code for examples Ask in Discord Open a discussion on GitHub

title: Template System
description: How Wails v3 scaffolds new projects, how templates are organised, and how to build your own.
text: Wails ships with a template system that lets wails3 init produce a ready-to-run project. A deliberately small set of frameworks have built-in templates (Vanilla, React, Vue, Svelte); any other framework can be used by bringing your own frontend or publishing a custom template . This page covers: Template directory layout How the CLI chooses & renders templates Creating a new template step-by-step Updating or overriding existing templates Troubleshooting and best practices 1. Where Templates Live text Copy v3/internal/templates/ ├── _common/ # Files copied into EVERY project (Taskfile.yml, build/, etc.) ├── base/ # Backend-only "plain Go" base layer (frontend/ + NEXTSTEPS.md) ├── ios/ # iOS bootstrapper ├── vanilla/ vanilla-js/ # TypeScript (default) + JavaScript variant ├── react/ react-js/ # TypeScript (default) + JavaScript variant ├── vue/ # TypeScript only ├── svelte/ # TypeScript only └── templates.go # Registry + Install/Get APIs (no auto-registration via embed) _common/ — universal boilerplate (Taskfile, build/ directory, shared infrastructure) merged into every project. base/ — the Go side that every template starts from. Note: base/ itself does not contain a template.json ; that file lives inside each framework-specific template. Framework folders — contain the frontend ( frontend/ ), framework config, and a template.json describing the template metadata. Folder names match the template ID you pass to the CLI ( wails3 init -t react ). Language convention: TypeScript is the default and owns the bare name ( react ); a JavaScript variant, where one exists, is suffixed -js ( react-js ). Built-in templates declare their language explicitly with typescript: true|false in template.yaml . Community templates may still use the legacy -ts suffix, which is honoured as a fallback. The whole internal/templates/ directory is compiled into the CLI binary via //go:embed * , so users can scaffold projects offline. 2. How wails3 init Uses Templates Call chain (no cmd/wails3/init.go — the CLI is wired up directly in cmd/wails3/main.go ): text Copy cmd/wails3/main.go (clir wiring) │ ▼ internal/commands/init.go Init(options *flags.Init) error │ ▼ internal/templates/templates.go │ templates.Install(options) │ templates.GetDefaultTemplates() ▼ gosod.New(template.FS).Extract(options.ProjectDir, data) // file extraction │ ▼ go mod tidy (unless --skipgomodtidy / -skipgomodtidy) There is no Template.Load() / Template.CopyTo() / Template.Validate() API — extraction is handled by gosod ( github.com/leaanthony/gosod ) against the embedded fs.FS . wails3 init flags Defined in internal/flags/init.go : Flag Purpose Default -p Package name main -t Built-in template name, local path, or URL vanilla -n Project name (empty) -d Project directory . -q Suppress console output false -l List templates false -skipgomodtidy Skip running go mod tidy after extraction false -git Git repository URL to initialise (empty) -mod Go module path (derived from -git if not set) (empty) -s Skip the warning when using remote templates false -productname / -productdescription / -productversion / -productcompany / -productcopyright / -productcomments / -productidentifier Metadata baked into the generated build assets sensible defaults There is no -list long alias ( -l only) and no per-template --help . Substitutions Placeholders are standard Go template directives — the leading . is part of the field accessor: Placeholder Example Source {{.ProjectName}} myapp -n flag / directory name {{.ModulePath}} github.com/me/myapp -mod flag or derived from -git {{.WailsVersion}} v3.0.0-… Compiled-in constant from internal/version {{.ProductName}} , {{.ProductDescription}} , {{.ProductVersion}} , {{.ProductCompany}} , {{.ProductCopyright}} , {{.ProductComments}} , {{.ProductIdentifier}} Bake-time metadata corresponding -product* flags If you need a new placeholder, add a field to the template data in internal/templates/templates.go and a matching field/flag in internal/flags/init.go (or set it from internal/commands/init.go ). Post-Copy Hook After gosod finishes extracting the template, the CLI runs: text Copy go mod tidy unless you pass -skipgomodtidy . There is no task deps step. 3. Creating a New Template Example: Add a Solid template 3.1 Folder & ID text Copy internal/templates/solid/ The folder name = template ID. Keep it kebab-case . 3.2 Minimal File Set text Copy solid/ ├── template.yaml # name, description, wailsVersion, typescript (required) ├── frontend/ # Your web project (no node_modules/dist) │ ├── src/ │ ├── package.json │ └── vite.config.ts └── ... # Any extra Go files the template wants to inject Start by copying react and pruning files. Don’t forget to author a template.yaml — set typescript: true for a TypeScript template — base/ is the only folder without one. 3.3 Update Placeholders Search/replace literal sample values for Go template directives, e.g.: myapp → {{.ProjectName}} github.com/you/myapp → {{.ModulePath}} 3.4 Wire Up Because templates.go walks the embedded FS at init time, dropping a new folder under internal/templates/<id>/ is generally sufficient — no manual registration call is required. If you need extra logic (custom validation, post-copy steps), add it to templates.Install in internal/templates/templates.go . 3.5 Test bash Copy wails3 init -n demo -t solid cd demo wails3 dev Ensure: Dev server starts on the port published in WAILS_VITE_PORT Generated bindings appear under frontend/bindings/... Hot-reload works 4. Modifying Existing Templates Edit files under internal/templates/<id>/ . Rebuild the CLI ( cd v3 && go build -o ../wails3 ./cmd/wails3 ); the //go:embed * directive picks up the new content. Bump any dependency versions in frontend/package.json & Taskfile.yml . Update the template’s template.json description if behaviour changes. Common Tweaks Task Where Change dev server port frontend/vite.config.ts — read WAILS_VITE_PORT Add environment variables build/Taskfile.yml or frontend/.env Replace JS package manager Swap npm → pnpm / bun in build/Taskfile.yml 5. Template Authoring Tips Keep frontend generic — avoid referencing Wails-specific globals; /wails/runtime.js is served by the asset server at runtime. No compiled artefacts — exclude node_modules , dist , .DS_Store from the embedded directory (or .gitignore them so they’re never committed). Document prerequisites — Node version, extra CLI tools, etc., in template.json or NEXTSTEPS.md . Avoid breaking changes — if the overhaul is big, create a new template ID rather than mutating an existing one. 6. Troubleshooting Symptom Cause Fix unknown template name Typo in -t or template not embedded Run wails3 init -l to list available templates Placeholders not replaced Used {{ProjectName}} instead of {{.ProjectName}} Add the leading . (Go template field access) Dev server opens blank page Vite config not reading WAILS_VITE_PORT Check your vite.config.ts Frontend fails to build in prod Forgotten Vite base path Set base: "./" in vite.config.ts 7. Key Source File Map File Responsibility internal/templates/templates.go Embeds template FS, exposes Install(options *flags.Init) error , GetDefaultTemplates() , ValidTemplateName(name) internal/templates/<id>/** Actual template content internal/commands/init.go CLI glue: picks template, fills metadata, calls templates.Install internal/commands/generate_template.go wails3 generate template — utility to export a live project back into a template (handy for updates) internal/flags/init.go Flag definitions for wails3 init 8. Recap Templates live in internal/templates/ and are baked into the CLI via //go:embed * . wails3 init -t <id> extracts the template via gosod and runs go mod tidy (skippable with -skipgomodtidy ). Creating a template is as simple as making a folder , adding files plus a template.json , and using {{.ProjectName}} -style placeholders. The system is extensible and self-contained — perfect for sharing custom stacks with your team or the community. Happy templating!

title: Testing & Continuous Integration
description: How Wails v3 ensures quality with unit tests, integration suites, race detection, and GitHub Actions CI.
text: Robust desktop frameworks demand rock-solid testing. Wails v3 employs a layered strategy : Layer Goal Tooling Unit tests Fast feedback for isolated functions go test ./... Generator / CLI tests Validate wails3 generate bindings and the CLI plumbing task test:generator , task test:cli Template tests Make sure every shipped template still builds task test:templates Race detection Catch data races in the runtime & bridge go test -race ./... CI matrix Cross-OS confidence on every PR GitHub Actions This document explains where tests live , how to run them , and what the Taskfile orchestrates . The race guidance referenced by older drafts as pkg/application/RACE.md lives in v3/TESTING.md today. 1. Directory Conventions text Copy v3/ ├── internal/.../_test.go # Unit tests for internal packages ├── pkg/.../_test.go # Public API tests ├── tasks/events/generate.go # Code generator for event constants (NOT a test harness) ├── tests/ # Top-level integration test harness └── TESTING.md # Race / Cgo testing guidance Guidelines: Keep unit tests next to code ( foo.go ↔ foo_test.go ). Use the black-box style for pkg/ packages ( package application_test ) where it improves API hygiene. Shared fixtures live where they’re used (there is no central internal/testutil/ package in this tree — wire helpers per package instead). 2. Unit Tests Writing Tests go Copy func TestEventConstants (t * testing. T ) { assert. NotEmpty (t, events. Common . WindowFocus ) } Recommendations: Use stretchr/testify — already in go.mod . Prefer table-driven tests whenever several inputs, edge cases, or expected outcomes exercise the same behaviour. Give every case a descriptive name. Stub platform quirks behind build tags ( foo_windows_test.go , foo_darwin_test.go , …) when needed. Coverage expectation New and changed logic is expected to have 100% Go statement coverage. Measure the package you changed rather than relying on a repository-wide percentage: bash Copy go test ./pkg/application -coverprofile=coverage.out go tool cover -func=coverage.out Some paths are reasonably untestable in a normal test environment—for example, platform-only failures, hardware-dependent behaviour, or a defensive fallback that cannot be induced safely. Keep those exceptions narrow and explain each uncovered path in the PR description. Running Locally bash Copy cd v3 go test ./... -cover Or via Taskfile (real targets — there is no task test shortcut): text Copy task test:cli # CLI plumbing tests task test:generator # bindings generator round-trip tests task test:templates # build every shipped template task test:infrastructure # supporting helpers task test:examples # exercise the example matrix (downloads as needed) task test:all # everything above task sanity # quick smoke check (also: sanity:gtk4) task precommit # what you should run before pushing 3. Integration Tests v3/tests/ hosts the cross-package integration harness. The Taskfile test:example:* and test:examples:* targets drive build-and-launch checks across darwin / windows / linux (including Docker-based GTK3 / GTK4 matrices on Linux). Runnable examples live in v3/examples/ . The test targets select and build the examples appropriate to the host platform or CI matrix. Run the host-platform smoke suite with: text Copy task test:examples # host task test:examples:all # full matrix (slow) 4. Race Detection Data races are fatal in GUI runtimes. Race Guide See v3/TESTING.md for: Known benign races and suppression rationale How to interpret stack-traces crossing Cgo boundaries (Linux GTK + WebKit2GTK) Local Race Suite text Copy go test -race ./... wails3 dev has no -race flag — its CLI flags are --config , --port , and -s (enable HTTPS). To exercise the runtime under the race detector, build a test app with go build -race and run it directly. 5. GitHub Actions Workflows Real workflow files under .github/workflows/ (verified against the tree): File Purpose build-and-test-v3.yml Main v3 build + test matrix. Uses actions/setup-go@v5 with go-version: 1.25 . Runs task runtime:check , task runtime:test , task runtime:build , task test:examples (and BUILD_TAGS=gtk4 task test:examples for the GTK4 path), task generator:test:check , task install , then wails3 build as a smoke check. Linux jobs install libgtk-3-dev libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev libwayland-dev build-essential pkg-config xvfb x11-xserver-utils at-spi2-core xdg-desktop-portal-gtk and run the test suite under dbus-run-session -- xvfb-run . cross-compile-test-v3.yml Cross-compile sanity checks auto-changelog-v3.yml , changelog-v3.yml Changelog automation nightly-release-v3.yml Nightly v3 release artefacts bump-webview2-v3.yml , release-webview2.yml WebView2 dependency / release management build-cross-image.yml Builds the cross-compiler container image publish-npm.yml Publishes the embedded @wailsio/runtime JS runtime to npm pr-master.yml PR-side checks against the master branch semgrep.yml Semgrep static analysis stale-issues.yml , issue-labeler.yml , file-labeler.yml , claude.yml , generate-sponsor-image.yml , sync-translated-documents.yml , upload-source-documents.yml , build-and-test.yml , weekly-release-v2.yml Repo-housekeeping / v2-side flows There is no qodana.yaml and no runtime.yml in this tree — older drafts of this page named both, but only semgrep.yml covers static analysis and the runtime JS package is published through publish-npm.yml . The CI steps mirror the Taskfile targets above ( task test:cli , task test:generator , task test:templates , task test:examples , …) so you can reproduce CI locally one-to-one. The smoke wails3 build step in build-and-test-v3.yml is invoked with no extra flags — there is no -skip-package flag on wails3 build . 6. Local CI Parity There is no single task ci umbrella target. Reproduce CI by chaining the real targets: text Copy task precommit task test:cli task test:generator task test:templates task test:examples 7. Troubleshooting Failing Tests Symptom Likely Cause Fix Race in webview_window_darwin.go Mutating window state off the main thread Marshal through application.InvokeAsync / Invoke so the call runs on the main thread Linux test hangs in headless CI GTK needs a display Run under xvfb-run , e.g. xvfb-run task test:examples:linux Template build fails Frontend lockfile out of date Re-run wails3 init against a clean directory to refresh the template Coverpkg errors Integration test importing main Switch to build tag //go:build integration and gate the import 8. Adding New Tests Unit — create *_test.go , run go test ./... Generator / CLI — extend the cases under internal/generator/testcases/ or internal/commands/*_test.go and re-run task test:generator / task test:cli Templates / examples — make sure the shipped templates still build with task test:templates 9. Key File Map What Path Generator round-trip test internal/generator/generate_test.go Build-assets test internal/commands/build-assets_test.go Race / Cgo guide v3/TESTING.md Taskfile test targets v3/Taskfile.yaml Event-constants generator v3/tasks/events/generate.go CI workflow .github/workflows/build-and-test-v3.yml (Go 1.25 via actions/setup-go@v5 ) Static analysis .github/workflows/semgrep.yml Runtime npm publish .github/workflows/publish-npm.yml Quality isn’t an afterthought in Wails v3. With unit tests, generator/template suites, race detection, and a cross-platform CI matrix you can contribute confidently, knowing your changes run green on every OS we support. Happy testing!
